technical: A pipeline that captures the audio of a clinical encounter, runs automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization, and passes the resulting transcript to a language model that generates a structured note. The model output is conditioned on a note template and often on chart context pulled from the EHR, and it is written back through an EHR integration rather than existing as free text.
intuitive: A microphone in the room listens to the visit and drafts your note for you. It is not transcribing what you said into the note, it is summarizing a conversation, which means it can compress, reorder, or quietly invent detail that nobody spoke aloud.
clinical: You are the author of record on a note you did not write, so the attestation you sign covers hallucinated history and omitted negatives just as fully as anything you typed yourself.

technical: Software that takes patient-specific data and returns an assessment, risk score, or recommendation intended to inform a clinician's decision. In United States regulation the term is also a legal category: the 21st Century Cures Act excludes certain CDS from the device definition only if the software does not analyze a signal or image, and if the clinician can independently review the basis for the recommendation.
intuitive: Anything that looks at this patient and tells you something about them, from a sepsis alert to a risk calculator to a chatbot answering a question about the chart. The regulatory line turns on whether you can see and check the reasoning, not on how smart the tool is.
clinical: The exclusion that keeps a tool out of FDA oversight depends on you being able to independently review its basis, which is exactly the property most opaque machine learning models do not have.

technical: Assessment of a model on data from a source not used in development, differing in site, time period, population, or measurement process. It quantifies both discrimination and calibration under distribution shift, and calibration typically degrades first and more severely than discrimination, which is why reporting AUC alone conceals most transportability failure.
intuitive: Test the model somewhere it has never been. A model learns the habits of the hospital that trained it, including which patients get which tests ordered, and those habits do not travel.
clinical: The Epic sepsis model is the standing example: strong internal numbers, and on external validation it missed most sepsis cases while generating alerts on a large fraction of hospitalized patients.

technical: Evaluation of a model on patients enrolled after the model is fixed, with outcomes ascertained forward in time and predictions generated under deployment conditions. It is the only design that measures performance in the presence of real-time data availability, real case mix, and, when the output is shown, the clinician response that the model induces.
intuitive: Lock the model, then watch what happens to the next patients. Retrospective testing asks whether the model could have been right about the past; prospective testing asks whether it is right about the future, which is a harder and different question.
clinical: Very few marketed clinical AI tools have prospective evidence and almost none have randomized outcome data, so when a vendor cites validation, the first question is whether any patient was ever enrolled after the model was frozen.

technical: A per-pixel or per-region attribution overlay indicating which parts of an input image most influenced a model output, computed from gradients, activations, or occlusion. Standard saliency methods fail basic sanity checks, in that some produce visually similar maps for a trained network and one with randomized weights, and in medical imaging they localize known abnormalities substantially worse than human annotators.
intuitive: The colored blob on the chest film showing where the model supposedly looked. It is tempting to read it as the model's reasoning, but a blob over the right lung is consistent with the model having keyed on the laterality marker, the projection, or the scanner.
clinical: A plausible-looking heatmap over the correct lesion is not evidence the model found the lesion, and radiology AI evaluations that grade maps against expert segmentations generally find poor agreement.

technical: A deployment stage in which a model runs on live production data at the real prediction time, with outputs logged but withheld from clinicians. It tests the full data pipeline under real-time conditions, including feature availability and timing, and yields prospective performance estimates without exposing patients to the model's recommendations.
intuitive: Turn the model on but do not show anyone what it says, then look at the log later and ask how it did. It catches the failures that only appear in the real pipeline, such as a lab value that is available in the research dataset but not yet resulted when the alert would have fired.
clinical: This is the step most often skipped between a promising retrospective AUC and an alert in your workflow, and it is where models that looked excellent on curated data usually reveal that their key input arrives too late to be useful.

technical: The probability that a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, equal to the area under the sensitivity versus 1 minus specificity curve. It is invariant to prevalence and to any monotone rescaling of the score, which is precisely why it is a weak safety argument: a model can have an excellent AUROC and be badly miscalibrated, and AUROC gives equal weight to threshold regions no clinician would ever operate in.
intuitive: The C-statistic, with the same meaning you already use for risk models. The ML-specific misuse is treating it as the headline safety metric. Because it only measures ranking, it says nothing about whether the model's stated probabilities are trustworthy and nothing about performance at the one threshold you will actually deploy at.
clinical: Deployment decisions need sensitivity, specificity, and PPV at the chosen threshold plus a calibration plot; an AUROC of 0.90 is compatible with an alert that is wrong four times out of five in practice.

technical: The fraction of predictions that match the reference label. For balanced multiple-choice benchmarks it is a reasonable summary; for imbalanced detection tasks it is dominated by the majority class and a constant predictor can score highly. For generative models, accuracy usually means exact string match after normalization, which conflates format errors with reasoning errors and is highly sensitive to the answer parser.
intuitive: Percent correct. With a rare condition, always saying no gets you a high percent correct and catches nobody, which is why a single accuracy number is often the least informative thing on a results slide.
clinical: The accuracy paradox is the familiar prevalence trap: a model reported at 97 percent accuracy on a 2 percent prevalence outcome may be worse than useless.

technical: A fixed dataset paired with a scoring function and a decoding protocol, used to produce a comparable scalar score across models. A benchmark score is only interpretable relative to its specific prompt format, answer parser, few-shot count, and decoding temperature, all of which can move results by several points without any change in underlying capability. Aggregate leaderboard numbers therefore measure a model-plus-harness system, not a model.
intuitive: A standardized test for a model, closer to a board exam than to a clinical rotation. It tells you how the model does on this exact set of questions asked in this exact way, and very little about how it does on your patients in your workflow.
clinical: A vendor citing a benchmark score is telling you about performance on a test set assembled by someone else, which is roughly as informative as a drug's performance in a trial population you have not seen the inclusion criteria for.

technical: Presence of benchmark test items, or near-duplicates of them, in a model's pretraining corpus, which converts a generalization test into a memorization test. Detection is hard because pretraining corpora are usually undisclosed; proxies include n-gram overlap searches, perplexity gaps between canonical and perturbed phrasings, and ordering effects in multiple-choice options. Rephrased or translated variants evade standard n-gram decontamination while still inflating scores substantially.
intuitive: The model may have seen the exam before. Since these systems were trained on a large fraction of the public internet, and question banks and their answers live on the public internet, a strong score on an old benchmark can reflect recall of the answer key rather than reasoning.
clinical: This is the specific reason to distrust USMLE-style scores as evidence of clinical reasoning: those question banks and their explanations were on the web well before the model was trained.

technical: A model is calibrated if among all cases assigned probability p, a fraction p are positive. It is assessed with calibration curves, calibration slope and intercept, or expected calibration error, and it is orthogonal to discrimination. Modern deep networks are systematically overconfident, and post-hoc temperature scaling or isotonic regression fixes the average without fixing subgroup calibration. For language models, the reported verbal confidence and the token-level probability are different objects, and instruction-tuned or RLHF-trained models are notably worse calibrated than their base models.
intuitive: Whether a stated 70 percent actually means 70 percent. Two additional ML-specific traps: recalibrating on the whole population can leave a subgroup badly off, and when a chatbot writes I am 90 percent confident, that sentence is generated text with no reliable connection to any internal probability.
clinical: Calibration is what determines whether a model's risk output can be fed into a threshold-based decision at all, and it is the first thing to degrade when a model is moved to a new site or left running for a year.

aliases: does the benchmark measure what it claims
technical: The degree to which an operationalized measurement captures the abstract construct it claims to measure. In ML evaluation the construct, for example clinical reasoning, is unobservable and the measurement, for example MedQA accuracy, is a convenient proxy; construct validity asks how tight that link is. Failures include capability constructs defined post hoc by whichever dataset exists, benchmarks whose items admit shortcut solutions, and label definitions that encode a proxy target such as healthcare cost standing in for health need.
intuitive: Whether the test measures the thing its name implies. A benchmark called clinical reasoning that consists of multiple-choice recall is measuring something real, just not clinical reasoning, and once a number has a name people argue about the number rather than about what it stands for.
clinical: The Obermeyer analysis is the canonical medical example: an algorithm labeled to predict health needs actually predicted healthcare spending, and because less money is spent on Black patients at equal illness, the proxy encoded large racial bias.

aliases: harmonic mean of precision and recall
technical: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR over P plus R. It is a single-threshold summary that ignores true negatives entirely, is not symmetric under swapping the positive and negative class, and implicitly asserts that a false positive and a false negative are equally costly. Macro-F1 averages per-class F1 with equal class weight, micro-F1 pools counts and reduces to accuracy in single-label settings, and the two can rank models in opposite orders.
intuitive: One number that splits the difference between PPV and sensitivity. It is convenient for ranking models on a leaderboard and a poor basis for a clinical decision, because it silently assumes that missing a case and raising a false alarm hurt the same amount, which is almost never true in medicine.
clinical: Any F1-based claim should prompt the question of what the model's operating threshold was and whether the implied one-to-one cost ratio between missed cases and false alarms matches your setting.

technical: The reference labels a model is scored against. In practice ground truth is almost never the true state of nature but a proxy produced by human annotators, billing codes, natural language processing over notes, or consensus panels, each with its own error rate and systematic bias. When annotator agreement is imperfect, measured model accuracy is bounded by label quality, and a model can be penalized for being right against a wrong label.
intuitive: The answer key. The uncomfortable part is that the key was written by people or extracted from administrative data, so it has its own errors and its own blind spots baked in, and the model is being graded against those errors as well as against reality.
clinical: This is the reference standard problem from diagnostic accuracy studies, and it bites hard in AI because ICD codes, radiology report text, and single-reader labels are routinely treated as if they were histopathology.

technical: Data withheld from training and used to estimate generalization error. The estimate is unbiased only for a single, pre-specified evaluation; every subsequent decision made in response to holdout performance leaks information from the holdout into the model, so repeated use converts the test set into a training set by slow degrees. Standard practice therefore splits into a development set for iteration and a test set touched once.
intuitive: The questions you deliberately did not study, kept sealed so you can find out whether you actually learned the material. The catch is that if you peek, adjust, and re-take, the seal is broken, even though the numbers still look like an honest exam score.
clinical: Internal holdout performance is analogous to apparent validity in a derivation cohort, and like a prediction rule it means little until externally validated at another site and time period.

technical: Scoring model outputs with human raters against a defined rubric, reported with inter-rater reliability and, ideally, blinding and randomized presentation order. It is the reference method for open-ended generation because automated metrics do not detect fluent falsehoods. Its weaknesses are cost, small sample sizes leading to wide confidence intervals, rubric underspecification, and rater preference for fluent and lengthy answers regardless of correctness.
intuitive: Having actual clinicians read the model's answers and rate them. It is the only evaluation that directly asks the question you care about, and it is expensive enough that most studies use a few hundred items and a handful of raters, so the error bars are usually much wider than the reported point estimate suggests.
clinical: Look for blinding, the number and specialty of raters, inter-rater agreement, and whether raters saw the model's answer next to a physician's answer, since unblinded raters reliably prefer the more polished text.

technical: Using a language model to score or rank the outputs of another model, usually with a rubric prompt and either a pointwise rating or a pairwise preference. Judges exhibit reproducible biases: position bias favoring the first option, verbosity bias favoring longer answers, self-preference for outputs from the same model family, and poor sensitivity to factual errors that are stated fluently. Agreement with expert humans is often reported as roughly 80 percent on general tasks, which is close to human-human agreement but is measured on tasks where errors are easy to see.
intuitive: Having one model grade another's homework because hiring physicians to grade thousands of answers is slow and expensive. It works reasonably for style and structure and is least reliable exactly where it matters most, which is catching a confidently written falsehood in a specialist domain the judge does not know well.
clinical: If a medical AI product reports safety or accuracy metrics graded by another model rather than by clinicians, treat that as a screening result and not as evidence of clinical validity.

technical: A 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark spanning humanities, STEM, law, and several medical subjects, scored as accuracy over roughly 14,000 test items. It is evaluated few-shot and is dominated by factual recall rather than reasoning depth. It contains known label errors and ambiguous items, so the practical ceiling is below 100 percent, and it is among the most contaminated benchmarks in wide use.
intuitive: A very broad trivia and reasoning exam covering everything from clinical knowledge to jurisprudence. It is useful as a rough general-knowledge thermometer and close to useless for distinguishing two strong models, because at the top of the range the remaining errors are mostly bad questions.
clinical: MMLU includes clinical knowledge, anatomy, and professional medicine subsets that vendors sometimes quote as evidence of medical competence, which they are not.

technical: A multiple-choice question answering dataset drawn from professional medical licensing examinations, most commonly the US Medical Licensing Examination subset used in English. Models are scored on exact-match selection of one of four or five options, typically with few-shot prompting or chain-of-thought decoding. It has become the de facto headline metric for medical language models despite being a closed-form recall and reasoning test.
intuitive: A model taking Step-style questions. It is a real test of medical knowledge and single-step reasoning, but the questions come with a curated vignette, a clean stem, and a guaranteed correct option on the page, none of which describe an actual patient encounter.
clinical: High MedQA scores establish that a model has book knowledge, not that it can take a history, tolerate missing data, or know when to stop and ask.

technical: Recall equals sensitivity, TP over TP plus FN. Precision equals positive predictive value, TP over TP plus FP. The ML convention differs from the clinical one in emphasis: ML reports precision and recall as a pair at a chosen operating threshold and summarizes the tradeoff with average precision or area under the precision-recall curve, which unlike AUROC changes with prevalence and is therefore preferred for rare-positive detection tasks.
intuitive: Recall is the same quantity you know as sensitivity. Precision is the same quantity you know as PPV. The important difference is habit rather than mathematics: ML papers quote precision as if it were a property of the model, when it depends on prevalence exactly as PPV does, so a precision figure from a curated dataset does not transfer to your clinic.
clinical: A vendor reporting 0.85 precision on a balanced research set is quoting a PPV that will collapse when the model meets real prevalence, which is the single most common way AI performance claims mislead.

technical: Adversarial probing of a system to elicit harmful, false, or policy-violating behavior, performed manually by humans, automatically by an attacker model, or by hybrid pipelines. Unlike a benchmark it produces existence proofs rather than rates: it establishes that a failure is reachable, not how often it occurs in normal use. Coverage is the central methodological problem, since results reflect the imagination and domain expertise of the red team.
intuitive: Deliberately trying to make the system misbehave, similar to a failure mode and effects analysis or a simulated code scenario. A clean red team report means nobody found the problem, which is weaker evidence than it sounds, because the people probing rarely include a subspecialist thinking about your specific edge cases.
clinical: For a clinical deployment, the useful red team includes clinicians generating realistic bad inputs such as ambiguous drug names, contradictory chart data, and requests that should trigger escalation rather than an answer.

aliases: true positive rate and true negative rate
technical: Sensitivity is TP over TP plus FN and specificity is TN over TN plus FP, both computed at a specific operating threshold. In ML pipelines the threshold is frequently chosen on the same data used to report performance, which optimistically biases both figures, and the default 0.5 cutoff is an arbitrary artifact of the loss function rather than a clinically reasoned choice. Reported values also apply only to the spectrum of cases in the evaluation set, so a model tuned on a case-enriched dataset carries a spectrum bias into deployment.
intuitive: The same quantities you use for diagnostic tests, with two ML-specific caveats. First, the cutoff that produced them was often picked to make the numbers look good on the very data being reported. Second, deep models are not fixed tests: their sensitivity and specificity shift when the scanner, the coding practice, or the case mix changes, in a way a serum assay does not.
clinical: Ask which threshold was used, whether it was pre-specified, and what the case spectrum was, exactly as you would interrogate a STARD-reported diagnostic accuracy study.

technical: Excessive weighting of an initial value or hypothesis, with insufficient adjustment as new evidence arrives. In AI-assisted workflows it appears in two directions. The clinician anchors on the model's first suggestion and narrows the differential prematurely. The model anchors on framing in the prompt or on its own earlier tokens, since autoregressive generation conditions every subsequent token on what it already committed to, so an early wrong step tends to be elaborated rather than corrected.
intuitive: The cognitive bias you already know, now with a second party that has it too. The model-side version is specific: once it has written a wrong first sentence, everything after is generated conditional on that sentence being right, which is why a chain of reasoning can be internally coherent and wrong from step one.
clinical: Reading the model's suggested diagnosis before forming your own differential imports the bias directly, which argues for generating your own assessment first and consulting the model second.

technical: The tendency of human operators to over-accept automated recommendations, producing commission errors when they follow an incorrect suggestion and omission errors when they fail to detect a problem the system did not flag. It is a property of the human-model system rather than of the model, so it is invisible to standalone model evaluation and appears only in studies with human users in the loop. Empirically it is worse under time pressure, worse for less experienced users, and worse when confidence is displayed without calibration evidence.
intuitive: Trusting the machine more than it has earned. It cuts both ways: acting on a wrong alert, and failing to act because no alert fired. Notably, a model can improve average performance while degrading the performance of the clinicians who were already better than it, if they defer to it.
clinical: This is why standalone accuracy is the wrong endpoint and why prospective human-in-the-loop evaluation, as DECIDE-AI and CONSORT-AI require, is the evidence that actually matters.

technical: Loss of previously acquired capability when a network is trained on a new task, because gradient updates overwrite the weights encoding the old behavior. Mitigations include regularizing weights important to prior tasks, as in elastic weight consolidation, replaying original training data during fine-tuning, and parameter-efficient methods such as adapters or LoRA that leave base weights frozen. It is the main reason a model fine-tuned narrowly on institutional data can become worse at general reasoning and at safety behaviors it previously had.
intuitive: Teaching the model something new can erase something old. Unlike a person who gets rusty gradually and knows it, a network can lose a capability abruptly and completely while giving no sign, so the loss shows up only if you re-test for it.
clinical: If a vendor fine-tunes a model on your institution's notes, the resulting model needs full re-evaluation, not just evaluation on the new task, because safety behavior and general medical reasoning can both have degraded.

technical: A proposed narrower term for the subset of hallucinations that are arbitrary and unstable, meaning the model produces different wrong answers to the same question across samples because it lacks the knowledge rather than because it has learned something false. Confabulations are detectable by measuring semantic entropy over sampled answers, since sampling the same prompt repeatedly and clustering the answers by meaning reveals high entropy where the model is guessing. Systematic errors from bad training data are not confabulations and are not detectable this way.
intuitive: The specific case where the model does not know and improvises, filling the gap smoothly rather than saying so. The borrowing from neurology is deliberate and reasonably apt: it is gap-filling without awareness of the gap, not deception. The practical consequence is that asking the same question five times and getting five different answers is a usable warning sign.
clinical: Consistency across repeated queries is a cheap bedside check, and a good reason to be more suspicious of a specific number that changes when you ask again than of one that does not.

technical: A difference between the joint distribution of inputs and labels at training time and at deployment. Conventional subtypes are covariate shift, where the input distribution changes but the conditional label distribution does not, label shift, where prevalence changes, and concept shift, where the input to label relationship itself changes. Deep models degrade under shift far more than their in-distribution metrics suggest, and often fail silently because confidence does not drop when accuracy does.
intuitive: The model meets patients unlike those it learned from: a different scanner, a different referral pattern, a different documentation style, a different prevalence. The dangerous property is silence. Performance drops but the model keeps producing equally confident output, so nothing in the interface signals that it is now out of its depth.
clinical: This is the mechanism behind most failed external validations, including models that learn a scanner signature or a chest tube marker rather than the pathology itself.

technical: Generation of content that is unsupported by the source or by fact while remaining fluent and syntactically well formed. The literature distinguishes intrinsic hallucination, which contradicts a provided source, from extrinsic hallucination, which adds unverifiable content. It is not a bug in the usual sense but a consequence of training a model to maximize the likelihood of plausible continuations with no term in the objective for truth, and it cannot be fully eliminated by scale or by retrieval alone.
intuitive: The model produces something that reads exactly like a correct answer but is invented. The important property is that fluency and correctness are independent: there is no stylistic tell, and fabricated citations, doses, and guideline numbers arrive in the same confident register as accurate ones.
clinical: Fabricated references, invented trial results, and plausible but wrong dosing are the recurring pattern, and they are most dangerous in exactly the situation where a clinician is least able to check, which is outside their own specialty.

technical: An input crafted to make a model produce output its safety training was intended to suppress. Mechanistically it exploits two structural weaknesses: competing objectives, where helpfulness and instruction-following pull against the safety constraint, and mismatched generalization, where the pretraining distribution covers inputs such as base64, low-resource languages, or role-play frames that safety fine-tuning did not. Gradient-based search can produce transferable adversarial suffixes that work across models the attacker never queried.
intuitive: Wording a request so the model's guardrails do not recognize it, usually by wrapping it in fiction, a hypothetical, an authority claim, or an encoding. The relevant lesson is that guardrails are a trained tendency rather than an enforced rule, so they degrade under pressure instead of holding firm.
clinical: Assume a patient-facing medical chatbot can be talked into unsafe output, and design the deployment so that harm requires more than the model saying the wrong thing.

reading.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?
reading.note: the competing objectives and mismatched generalization framing

reading.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
reading.note: automatically discovered suffixes that transfer across models

technical: Degradation of a deployed model's performance over time, driven by changes in case mix, documentation and coding practice, upstream system upgrades, treatment guidelines, or by the model's own effect on care, which alters the outcomes it was trained to predict. Calibration typically degrades before discrimination, so AUROC monitoring alone misses it. The self-influence pathway, sometimes called performative prediction, means a successful model can invalidate its own training relationship.
intuitive: A model that worked at go-live quietly gets worse. Sometimes the world changed, sometimes the EHR build changed, and sometimes the model itself changed practice: if the sepsis alert works and people act on it, the sepsis outcomes it learned from no longer occur, which undermines the model. Silent updates from the vendor are a separate and equally real cause.
clinical: Deployed models need scheduled revalidation and calibration monitoring the way an analyzer needs QC, and any vendor model update should be treated as a new device rather than a patch.

reading.title: Calibration drift in regression and machine learning models for acute kidney injury
reading.note: shows calibration degrading over time while discrimination looks stable

reading.title: The Clinician and Dataset Shift in Artificial Intelligence
reading.note: covers drift sources specific to health system operations

technical: Variation in output across identical inputs. The intended source is stochastic decoding, where temperature and top-p sampling draw from the token distribution. A second and less appreciated source persists even at temperature zero: floating point non-associativity combined with batch-size-dependent reduction order in GPU kernels means the same prompt can yield different logits depending on what else is being served concurrently. Additional variation comes from silent model version updates and from changes to hidden system prompts.
intuitive: Ask the same question twice and get different answers. Some of that is deliberate randomness that can be turned down, but not all of it: the arithmetic on the server depends on how requests happen to be batched, and the vendor may swap the underlying model without telling you. So an output you validated last month may not be reproducible today.
clinical: This complicates validation and medicolegal documentation, since you cannot assume that regenerating a summary will reproduce what was originally shown, which argues for storing the actual output rather than the prompt.

reading.title: An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation
reading.note: measures output variance across repeated identical requests

reading.title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
reading.note: explains batch-invariance and why temperature zero is still not reproducible

technical: An attack in which instructions embedded in data that the model ingests are executed as if they were instructions from the operator or user. It is a consequence of the architecture: prompt and retrieved content occupy the same token stream with no privilege boundary, so there is no reliable equivalent of a parameterized query. Indirect injection is the dangerous form, where the payload sits in a document, web page, email, or scanned note that the system retrieves rather than in anything the user typed.
intuitive: Text inside a document the AI reads can hijack it, because the model cannot tell the difference between the content it was asked to read and the orders it was given. Distinct from jailbreaking: a jailbreak is the user attacking their own assistant, injection is a third party attacking the user's assistant through material the user trusted.
clinical: Relevant to any agent that reads referral letters, faxes, portal messages, or scanned outside records, since a crafted string in an incoming document could redirect what the agent writes or which tools it calls.

reading.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
reading.note: defines indirect prompt injection and demonstrates it end to end

reading.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
reading.note: practitioner risk list with prompt injection ranked first

technical: Declining to answer, produced by safety training rather than by any capability limit. The failure mode has two sides. Under-refusal answers requests that should be declined. Over-refusal declines benign requests that superficially resemble harmful ones, typically through keyword-level rather than intent-level generalization, and is measured by test suites of safe prompts that use unsafe-sounding vocabulary. Because helpfulness and harmlessness are optimized jointly, reducing one error rate generally increases the other.
intuitive: The model saying it cannot help. The clinically relevant failure is over-refusal: legitimate questions about overdose thresholds, self-harm risk assessment, controlled substance dosing, or termination of pregnancy get refused because the words look dangerous, even though the person asking is a clinician with an obvious professional reason.
clinical: A refusal is not a statement that the answer is unknown or that the question is inappropriate, and treating it as clinical guidance is a mistake; it usually means the request pattern-matched a safety filter.

reading.title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models
reading.note: benchmark of safe prompts that models wrongly refuse

reading.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
reading.note: documents the helpfulness versus harmlessness tension that produces refusals

technical: The tendency of a model to shift its stated answer toward the user's expressed belief, tone, or identity rather than toward the evidence. It arises predictably from preference-based training, since human raters reward responses that agree with them, so optimizing a reward model derived from those ratings selects for agreement. It is measurable: correct answers are frequently abandoned when a user simply expresses doubt, and the effect increases with model scale and with RLHF training.
intuitive: The model tends to agree with you. Push back on a correct answer and it will often apologize and give you the wrong one, not because it was persuaded but because agreement was rewarded during training. This is worse than a merely unreliable colleague, because an unreliable colleague at least errs in a direction independent of what you wanted to hear.
clinical: Leading a model with your working diagnosis in the prompt is close to worthless as a second opinion, and a model that folds when you express doubt is confirming your prior rather than testing it.

reading.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
reading.note: measures sycophancy across models and traces it to human preference data

reading.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
reading.note: finds sycophancy increases with scale and with RLHF steps

technical: A network interface through which an application sends inputs to a model hosted elsewhere and receives outputs, typically authenticated by key and billed per token. The operative consequence for regulated data is that inputs leave the institutional boundary and are governed by the provider's data retention, training-use, and subprocessor terms rather than by local controls.
intuitive: Your software calls someone else's model over the internet. Convenient and always up to date, but the text you send has left your building, and what happens to it afterward is a contract question.
clinical: Three questions decide whether an API is usable clinically: is there a signed BAA, is the data excluded from training, and how long is it retained, and all three are answered in the terms rather than in the product demo.

reading.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
reading.note: GPT-3, the model whose release established API-only access as the norm

reading.title: Business Associates
reading.note: the contractual condition for sending PHI to any hosted service

technical: Continued training of a model on institutional clinical text to adapt it to local vocabulary, note structure, and case mix. The trained weights become a derivative of the underlying data: models memorize and can emit verbatim training sequences, and membership inference can reveal whether a particular record was in the training set, so the resulting artifact must be governed as identifiable data rather than as anonymous parameters.
intuitive: Teaching the model on your own notes. The important and unintuitive part is that the model can regurgitate distinctive passages it was trained on, so the weights themselves carry patient information and are not a safely de-identified summary.
clinical: This is the step where an IRB submission, a data use agreement, and a security review all become necessary at once, and where sharing the resulting model with another institution is a disclosure rather than a software transfer.

reading.title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models
reading.note: demonstrates verbatim recovery of memorized training sequences

reading.title: Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models
reading.note: determining whether a specific record was in the training data

reading.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
reading.note: the parameter-efficient method most institutional fine-tuning actually uses

technical: A massively parallel processor with high memory bandwidth used to execute the dense matrix multiplications underlying neural network training and inference. For transformer inference the binding constraint is usually high-bandwidth memory: model weights, plus the key-value cache that grows with batch size and sequence length, must fit in device memory, which determines how many concurrent users a given card can serve.
intuitive: The specialized chip that makes these models run at usable speed. The number that matters is memory on the card, not raw speed, because the model weights and everyone's in-progress conversations have to sit in that memory at the same time.
clinical: This is why a self-hosted model in your own data center has a hard concurrency ceiling, and why the answer to how many clinicians can use it at once is a hardware question rather than a licensing one.

reading.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
reading.note: vLLM, showing key-value cache memory as the real serving bottleneck

reading.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
reading.note: why attention performance is governed by memory movement rather than arithmetic

technical: The marginal compute cost of generating a response, billed by hosted providers per input and output token with output typically priced several times higher than input. Cost scales with prompt length, so retrieval-augmented and long-chart workflows are dominated by input volume, and techniques such as prompt caching and batching change the economics substantially for repeated prefixes.
intuitive: You pay by the amount of text in and out, and pasting a whole chart in as context is the expensive part, not the paragraph that comes back. Costs that look trivial per note become real when multiplied by every encounter in a health system.
clinical: Ask a vendor whether per-encounter pricing includes the chart context they pull in, because that is where a per-note price quietly becomes a per-chart price.

reading.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
reading.note: serving efficiency gains that underlie hosted pricing

reading.title: Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference
reading.note: cost model for transformer inference at scale

technical: The delay between request and response, decomposable for language models into time to first token, dominated by prefill over the input, and inter-token latency during autoregressive decoding. Serving systems trade latency against throughput through batching, so a configuration tuned for cost per request will have worse tail latency than one tuned for interactive use.
intuitive: How long you wait. Long inputs make the first word slow, and long outputs make the rest slow, and a system tuned to serve many users cheaply will feel worse for any individual user.
clinical: The relevant number for a workflow tool is the ninety-fifth percentile, not the average, because a summarizer that usually takes two seconds and occasionally takes forty will be abandoned during a busy clinic.

reading.title: Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference
reading.note: lays out the latency versus throughput trade space for transformer serving

reading.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
reading.note: how batching and memory management determine achievable latency

technical: A model whose weights are obtained and executed on infrastructure the deploying organization controls, so no request data crosses an external boundary. Available open-weight models generally trail the strongest hosted frontier models in capability, and quantization used to fit them onto affordable hardware trades further accuracy for memory footprint.
intuitive: The model runs on your own machines. Nothing leaves, which solves a large class of privacy problems, and in exchange you get a somewhat weaker model plus responsibility for the hardware, updates, and monitoring.
clinical: Local deployment does not exempt you from validation or from HIPAA safeguards; it removes the vendor disclosure problem and hands you the operational and monitoring burden instead.

reading.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
reading.note: the release that made capable self-hostable weights broadly available

reading.title: On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models
reading.note: framework for the benefits and risks of downloadable weights

technical: Running inference inside infrastructure under the covered entity's administrative control, whether physical data center or a dedicated tenant in a cloud environment governed by the entity's own agreements. It changes the compliance analysis by keeping PHI inside the trust boundary, but the HIPAA Security Rule obligations for access control, audit logging, encryption, and integrity monitoring apply unchanged.
intuitive: The model runs on hardware you control, so patient data does not travel to a vendor. Note that in-cloud but inside your own tenancy is usually treated the same way, since the boundary that matters is contractual and administrative rather than geographic.
clinical: This is the arrangement most often demanded by security review for anything touching identified notes, and the realistic cost is dedicated GPUs plus the staff to keep them patched and monitored.

reading.title: Business Associates
reading.note: clarifies when a hosting arrangement makes a vendor a business associate

reading.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
reading.note: representative weights of the kind used for in-boundary deployments

technical: Open weights means downloadable parameters, which is sufficient to run and fine-tune a model locally but not to reproduce it. Open source in the traditional sense additionally requires the training data, training code, and a license without field-of-use restrictions, and most widely used open models meet the former and not the latter, often under community licenses with usage conditions.
intuitive: Most models called open give you the finished weights, not the recipe. You can run and adapt them, but you cannot inspect what they were trained on, which is precisely the thing you would want to audit before clinical use.
clinical: Open weights let you deploy inside your firewall without a vendor, but they do not tell you the training data, so provenance questions from an IRB or a compliance reviewer will still have no answer.

reading.title: The Open Source AI Definition
reading.note: the formal criteria distinguishing open source AI from downloadable weights

reading.title: On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models
reading.note: defines the openness gradient and analyses its consequences

reading.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
reading.note: a widely used open-weight release under a restricted community license

technical: A differentiable operation that computes an output as a weighted average of value vectors, where the weights come from a normalized similarity between a query vector and a set of key vectors. In scaled dot-product attention the weights are softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), which lets each position selectively pull information from any other position. Attention was introduced to let sequence models align source and target elements without compressing everything into a single fixed-size state.
intuitive: A mechanism that lets the model decide, for each word it is processing, which other words matter most and weight them accordingly. It is closer to a soft lookup than to human attention, and the weights are not an explanation of the model's reasoning.
clinical: Attention maps are often displayed as if they were an explanation of why a model flagged a finding, but they show where information was drawn from, not why a conclusion was reached.

reading.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
reading.note: introduced attention for sequence models

reading.title: Attention Is All You Need
reading.note: scaled dot-product and multi-head attention

technical: The maximum number of tokens a model can attend over in a single forward pass, spanning both the input and the generated output. It is bounded by the positional encoding scheme and by attention cost, which grows quadratically with sequence length in standard self-attention.
intuitive: Everything the model can hold in mind at once. Not a memory of past conversations, but a desk of fixed size: once it is full, something has to come off before anything else goes on.
clinical: A long discharge summary plus a full prior chart can exceed the window, and what falls off the desk is silently dropped rather than flagged.

reading.title: Attention Is All You Need
reading.note: the transformer paper that fixed attention as the core operation

reading.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
reading.note: shows accuracy degrades for information buried mid-context

technical: A generative model that defines a fixed forward process gradually adding Gaussian noise to data and learns a neural network to reverse it, producing samples by iterative denoising from pure noise. Training reduces to a simple regression objective on the noise added at each step, which is far more stable than adversarial training. Diffusion models dominate image and audio synthesis and increasingly appear in medical image reconstruction and synthetic data generation.
intuitive: The model learns to remove noise from an image, one small step at a time. To generate something new it starts from pure static and denoises repeatedly until a coherent picture appears.
clinical: Used for synthetic medical images and for accelerated MRI reconstruction, where the risk is plausible-looking anatomy that was hallucinated rather than measured.

reading.title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
reading.note: the original diffusion formulation

reading.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
reading.note: the simplification that made diffusion competitive for image generation

technical: A learned mapping from a discrete item such as a token, sentence or image patch into a dense real-valued vector space, in which geometric proximity encodes semantic or distributional similarity. Static embeddings assign one vector per word type, while contextual embeddings from a transformer assign a different vector to each occurrence depending on surrounding context. Embeddings are the substrate for similarity search, clustering and retrieval.
intuitive: A way of turning words or documents into lists of numbers so that things with similar meaning end up near each other. It is what lets a system recognize that myocardial infarction and heart attack are close, without anyone writing that rule down.
clinical: Embedding similarity powers most clinical retrieval and note deduplication tools, and it will happily rate a negated finding as similar to the affirmed one.

reading.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
reading.note: the word2vec paper that popularized learned word vectors

reading.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
reading.note: count-based alternative that clarified what the vector space encodes

technical: A model trained at scale on broad data with a self-supervised objective, intended to be adapted to many downstream tasks by fine-tuning, prompting or retrieval rather than trained from scratch per task. The defining properties are emergence, where capabilities appear that were not explicitly trained, and homogenization, where a single model becomes the shared substrate for many applications. The term is architecture-agnostic and covers language, vision and multimodal models.
intuitive: A general-purpose model trained once at enormous cost and then adapted cheaply to many uses. The efficiency is real, but so is the concentration of risk: a flaw in the base model propagates into every application built on it.
clinical: Because one base model may underlie your triage tool, your scribe and your patient portal chatbot, a single systematic bias can appear simultaneously across unrelated clinical workflows.

reading.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
reading.note: the report that coined and defined the term

technical: A neural network, almost always a transformer, trained on very large text corpora with a self-supervised objective such as next-token prediction, and typically holding billions of parameters. The trained model defines a probability distribution over the next token given the preceding sequence, and text is produced by repeatedly sampling from that distribution. Capabilities such as translation, summarization and reasoning emerge from this single objective rather than from task-specific supervision.
intuitive: A very large statistical model of language that has read an enormous amount of text and learned which words tend to follow which. It answers questions by generating the most plausible continuation of what you wrote, not by looking anything up in a database.
clinical: Every clinical chatbot, ambient scribe and note-summarization tool you are being sold is a wrapper around one of these, so its failure modes are the model's failure modes.

reading.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
reading.note: the GPT-3 paper, where scale alone produced general-purpose behavior

reading.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
reading.note: broad survey of what these models are and what they break

technical: An architecture in which the feed-forward block is replaced by many parallel expert subnetworks plus a learned router that dispatches each token to only a small number of them. Because only the selected experts run, total parameter count grows while per-token compute stays roughly constant, decoupling capacity from inference cost. The main engineering difficulties are load balancing across experts and the communication cost of routing in distributed training.
intuitive: Instead of one large network handling everything, the model keeps many specialist subnetworks and a dispatcher that sends each chunk of text to a couple of them. You get the knowledge of a huge model while paying to run only a slice of it.

reading.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
reading.note: the sparsely gated MoE layer

reading.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
reading.note: simplified top-1 routing that made MoE practical at scale

technical: A model that accepts or produces more than one data modality, typically by encoding each modality into a shared representation space and processing the combined token sequence with a single transformer. Common designs either align separately trained encoders with a contrastive objective or project image patch features into the token stream of a language model. Performance on any one modality is usually below that of a specialized unimodal model of similar size.
intuitive: A model that can take in pictures as well as text, by converting images into the same kind of numeric chunks it already uses for words. It is genuinely reading the image through a learned summary, not viewing it the way a radiologist does.
clinical: General multimodal models will confidently describe an ECG or a chest film, but they are not devices cleared for imaging interpretation and their error profile differs sharply from that of dedicated radiology models.

reading.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
reading.note: CLIP, the contrastive image-text alignment that underpins most VLMs

reading.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning
reading.note: interleaving image features into a frozen language model

technical: A parameterized function composed of alternating linear transformations and elementwise nonlinearities, arranged in layers and fit to data by gradient-based minimization of a loss. Depth allows hierarchical feature composition, and with sufficient width such networks are universal function approximators. The biological analogy is historical and does not describe how these systems actually compute.
intuitive: A stack of simple mathematical layers, each transforming numbers into other numbers, tuned until the whole stack maps inputs to the desired outputs. Despite the name it does not work like a brain in any meaningful sense.
clinical: Nearly all FDA-cleared AI imaging devices are neural networks, so their generalization limits across scanners and populations are the practical safety question.

reading.title: Deep learning
reading.note: the LeCun, Bengio and Hinton review

reading.title: Deep Learning
reading.note: the standard free textbook

technical: A release in which the trained parameters are published for download, allowing local inference, fine-tuning and inspection. Open weights is weaker than open source, since training data, training code and full recipes are usually withheld, and licenses may restrict commercial or downstream use. Once weights are distributed they cannot be recalled, and safety fine-tuning applied before release can be substantially undone with modest additional training.
intuitive: The model's numbers are published, so you can run it on your own hardware without sending data anywhere. It does not mean you know what it was trained on or can reproduce it.
clinical: This is the practical route to running an LLM entirely inside a hospital network so protected health information never leaves, at the cost of owning the validation and monitoring yourself.

reading.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
reading.note: the release that made capable open-weight models mainstream

reading.title: OLMo: Accelerating the Science of Language Models
reading.note: a genuinely open release including data and training code, not weights alone

technical: The learned numerical values, principally the weight matrices and biases of each layer, that are adjusted during training to minimize the loss. Parameter count is the standard shorthand for model capacity, though the compute-optimal balance between parameters and training tokens matters at least as much as raw count. Parameters are distinct from hyperparameters, which are set before training, and from activations, which are computed per input.
intuitive: The billions of adjustable numbers that make up the model. Training is the process of tuning them; the finished model is nothing but those numbers plus the code that runs them.
clinical: Parameter count is a poor proxy for clinical accuracy, and a smaller model tuned on relevant data often beats a larger general one on a specific task.

reading.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
reading.note: relates parameter count, data and compute to loss

reading.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
reading.note: the Chinchilla result that most large models were badly undertrained for their size

technical: Attention in which queries, keys and values are all linear projections of the same sequence, so every position attends over every other position of that same sequence. Multi-head self-attention runs several such projections in parallel in lower-dimensional subspaces and concatenates the results, letting different heads specialize in different relations. Cost and memory scale quadratically with sequence length, which is the principal constraint on context length.
intuitive: Each word in the passage compares itself to every other word in the same passage and builds a new representation of itself that reflects its neighbors. Doubling the length of the passage roughly quadruples the work.

reading.title: Attention Is All You Need
reading.note: defines multi-head self-attention and its quadratic cost

technical: The atomic discrete unit a language model consumes and emits, usually a subword fragment rather than a whole word, drawn from a fixed vocabulary of tens to hundreds of thousands of entries. Each token maps to an integer id and then to an embedding vector. Context limits, throughput and API pricing are all denominated in tokens, and one English word averages roughly 1.3 tokens.
intuitive: The chunks a model actually sees. Common words are one chunk, but a rare drug name may be split into four or five fragments, which is why models mangle unusual spellings and struggle to count letters.
clinical: Uncommon drug names, ICD codes and lab abbreviations fragment into many tokens, which degrades handling of exactly the terms clinical text is full of.

reading.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
reading.note: byte pair encoding, the origin of modern subword tokens

technical: The deterministic preprocessing step that segments raw text into tokens from a learned vocabulary, most commonly with byte pair encoding, WordPiece or unigram language model methods. The vocabulary is fit on a training corpus by greedily merging frequent character or byte sequences, so segmentation quality depends on how well that corpus matches deployment text. Tokenization is lossy in the sense that it fixes the granularity at which the model can reason about characters and numbers.
intuitive: The step that chops text into the pieces the model can handle, using a fixed dictionary of fragments built from ordinary web text. Text that looks nothing like that corpus, such as dense medical shorthand, gets chopped badly.
clinical: Numbers, dosages and lab values are split in inconsistent ways, which is one reason models make arithmetic and unit errors on clinical data.

reading.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
reading.note: introduces BPE for open-vocabulary text

reading.title: SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing
reading.note: the tokenizer implementation most current models build on

technical: A neural network architecture built from stacked blocks, each containing a multi-head self-attention layer and a position-wise feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization. It replaced recurrence with attention, so all positions in a sequence are processed in parallel and long-range dependencies are one attention hop apart rather than many recurrent steps. Position information is supplied explicitly through positional encodings or rotary embeddings.
intuitive: The blueprint underneath essentially every modern AI model. Its key trick is that every word in a passage can look directly at every other word at once, instead of reading strictly left to right and slowly forgetting the beginning.
clinical: It is the reason a model can connect a lab value on page one of a note to an assessment on page four, and also the reason cost rises steeply with document length.

reading.title: Attention Is All You Need
reading.note: the original transformer paper

reading.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
reading.note: the encoder-only variant that dominated clinical NLP for years

technical: An ordered list of real numbers treated as a point or direction in a high-dimensional space, and the basic data type moved through a neural network. Similarity between vectors is usually measured with cosine similarity or dot product, and nearly all neural computation reduces to matrix multiplications acting on batches of vectors. Dimensionality typically ranges from a few hundred to several thousand in current models.
intuitive: Just a list of numbers, but a list that locates an item in a space where distance means similarity. Think of a coordinate rather than a label.

reading.title: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality
reading.note: the follow-up word2vec paper on vector arithmetic over meaning

technical: A prompting strategy that induces the model to emit intermediate reasoning tokens before a final answer, effectively allocating more sequential computation to a problem. Gains are largest on multi-step arithmetic, symbolic and commonsense tasks and emerge mainly at larger model scales. The emitted trace is a generated artefact and is not guaranteed to be the causal path to the answer.
intuitive: Asking the model to show its working. Writing out the steps genuinely improves the final answer, but the written reasoning is a plausible narrative rather than a transcript of what the machine actually did, so a convincing chain can accompany a wrong conclusion.
clinical: A displayed differential-diagnosis rationale should be read as a claim requiring verification, not as an audit trail of how the answer was reached.

reading.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
reading.note: the originating paper

reading.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
reading.note: sampling many chains and taking a majority vote improves accuracy

reading.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
reading.note: generalises the linear chain into a searchable tree

technical: Placing a small number of input and output demonstrations in the context so that the model infers the task mapping at inference time. No weights change; the adaptation is a forward-pass phenomenon sometimes described as implicit inference over the demonstration distribution. Results are sensitive to example choice, ordering and label distribution, which introduces calibration artefacts.
intuitive: Showing the model two or three worked examples of what you want before asking your real question. It is teaching by demonstration within a single conversation, and nothing is retained afterwards.
clinical: Supplying a few correctly formatted prior notes is the cheapest way to make extraction or summarisation match local documentation conventions.

reading.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
reading.note: the original demonstration of in-context learning at scale

reading.title: Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
reading.note: quantifies how example order and formatting bias few-shot outputs

technical: Selecting the single highest-probability token at every step, equivalent to the zero-temperature limit of sampling. It is deterministic given fixed weights and prompt, but it optimises locally and can miss higher-likelihood complete sequences that require a lower-probability first token. It is also prone to repetition loops in open-ended generation.
intuitive: Always take the most likely next word. This makes output reproducible, which is useful for testing, but it can walk confidently down a dead end because it never looks past the immediate step.
clinical: Often the default for structured extraction from notes, where reproducibility matters more than fluency.

reading.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
reading.note: documents repetition and degeneration under maximisation-based decoding

technical: Executing a trained model on new input to produce output, with weights fixed. Autoregressive generation splits into a compute-bound prefill pass over the prompt and a memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase producing one token at a time, with a key-value cache holding attention state. Throughput and cost are dominated by cache management and batching, which is why serving systems such as PagedAttention focus on memory rather than arithmetic.
intuitive: The model actually running and answering, as opposed to being trained. Training happens once and costs a fortune; inference happens on every single query and is what you are billed for, which is why prompt length and output length translate directly into cost and latency.
clinical: Inference cost and latency, not model quality, usually decide whether an AI feature can run on every note in a busy clinic or only on request.

reading.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
reading.note: the vLLM paper on key-value cache management for high-throughput serving

reading.title: Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference
reading.note: partitioning and latency versus throughput trade-offs at scale

technical: The token sequence supplied to a language model as conditioning context before generation begins. The model computes a probability distribution over next tokens conditioned entirely on this sequence, so the prompt is the only channel through which task specification, instructions, examples and data reach the model at inference time. Prompt content is not persistent state: it must be resupplied on every call.
intuitive: Everything you hand the model in one go, including the instructions, the question and any background you paste in. The model has no memory outside of it, so if a fact is not in the prompt or in its training, it does not exist as far as the model is concerned.
clinical: If a patient's allergy list is not in the prompt, the model will not weigh it, and it will not tell you that it was missing.

reading.note: established prompting as the primary interface to large language models

reading.title: The Prompt Report: A Systematic Survey of Prompt Engineering Techniques

technical: A parameterised prompt string with named slots filled at runtime from user input, retrieved passages or structured data, producing a reproducible and versionable prompt. Templating is the unit of change control in an LLM application: template edits alter behaviour as materially as a model swap, and unescaped interpolation of untrusted content into a template is the primary prompt injection vector.
intuitive: A form letter with blanks that get filled in for each case, so every query is phrased the same way. It makes behaviour consistent and testable, and it is also where pasted patient text can smuggle in instructions the system then obeys.
clinical: Prompt templates should be version-controlled and revalidated like any other clinical decision support rule, because an untracked wording change can shift outputs across every user at once.

technical: A language model post-trained, typically with reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes, to produce extended internal deliberation before answering. Accuracy on hard mathematical, coding and diagnostic benchmarks scales with the length of that deliberation, trading latency and token cost for correctness. The reasoning trace may be hidden from the user or summarised.
intuitive: A model configured to think for longer before speaking, rather than answering on reflex. It is slower and more expensive per query, and the advantage appears mostly on genuinely hard multi-step problems rather than routine ones.
clinical: Worth the extra latency for complex diagnostic reasoning or guideline reconciliation, and largely wasted on note formatting or simple lookup.

technical: The procedure for selecting each successive token from the model's predicted next-token distribution. Common variants include greedy selection, beam search, temperature-scaled multinomial sampling and truncation methods such as top-k and top-p. Because generation is autoregressive, sampling choices compound: an early low-probability token conditions everything that follows.
intuitive: The model does not produce one answer, it produces odds over the next word, and the sampling rule decides which one is actually written. Ask twice and you can get two different answers from an identical model and prompt.
clinical: Nondeterminism means the same clinical question asked twice may yield different recommendations, which complicates both validation and medicolegal documentation.

reading.note: the standard comparison of decoding strategies

reading.title: Hierarchical Neural Story Generation

technical: Techniques that force generated text to conform to a formal specification such as a JSON Schema, regular expression or context-free grammar. Implementations mask disallowed tokens at each decoding step using a finite-state or pushdown automaton compiled from the schema, which guarantees syntactic validity at negligible cost. Syntactic conformance is guaranteed; semantic correctness of the field values is not.
intuitive: Making the model fill in a fixed form rather than write prose, enforced at the level of each character it emits so it literally cannot produce a malformed record. The boxes will always be filled and correctly shaped; whether the contents are true is a separate question.
clinical: This is how a model output becomes a structured problem list or a discrete lab value that a downstream system can consume, and it is where a fabricated value looks indistinguishable from a real one.

reading.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models
reading.note: finite-state machine formulation of regex and grammar constrained decoding

reading.title: Structured Outputs
reading.note: vendor documentation for schema-conforming generation

technical: A privileged instruction block placed at the head of the context, marked with a distinct role token, that specifies persona, constraints, output format and refusal behaviour for the whole session. Its elevated authority is a learned behaviour instilled by instruction tuning and preference optimisation, not a hard architectural guarantee, so sufficiently adversarial user content can override it.
intuitive: Standing orders written at the top of the chart that apply to every subsequent exchange. The model has been trained to treat them as more authoritative than what the user types, but that priority is a habit rather than a lock.
clinical: Vendor system prompts decide whether a clinical assistant hedges, cites, or refuses, and they are often invisible to the clinician using the tool.

reading.note: InstructGPT, the source of instruction-following and role hierarchy behaviour

technical: A scalar T that divides the logits before the softmax, so the sampling distribution becomes proportional to exp(z/T). Values below one sharpen the distribution toward high-probability tokens, values above one flatten it, and the limit as T approaches zero is greedy selection. Temperature alters output diversity but does not improve calibration or factual accuracy.
intuitive: A dial from cautious to adventurous. Turned low, the model keeps picking the safest next word and repeats itself; turned high, it takes more risks and invents more. Lowering it reduces variety, not error.
clinical: A low temperature makes a model reproducibly wrong rather than reliably right, so it is not a substitute for validation.

reading.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
reading.note: the standard reference for temperature scaling of a softmax

reading.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
reading.note: analyses how decoding parameters shape text quality

technical: Computation expended during inference rather than training, through longer generated reasoning, repeated sampling, search over candidates, or verifier-guided selection. Empirically, accuracy improves roughly log-linearly with additional inference compute on tasks with checkable structure, and on some budgets this outperforms spending the same compute on a larger model.
intuitive: Buying better answers by letting the model work longer or try several times, instead of buying a bigger model. The gain is real but bounded, and it costs time and money on every single query rather than once during training.
clinical: Explains why a careful diagnostic query can cost far more than a summarisation query against the same underlying model.

reading.note: the central empirical study of inference-time scaling

reading.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
reading.note: an early and simple form of spending extra compute at inference

technical: A truncated sampling scheme that restricts each draw to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability mass exceeds p, renormalises over that nucleus, and samples. Unlike fixed top-k truncation, the candidate set size adapts to the sharpness of the distribution, which suppresses the unreliable tail without over-constraining genuinely ambiguous positions.
intuitive: Before each word, the model discards the long tail of implausible options and chooses only among the ones that together account for most of the probability. The size of that shortlist changes automatically depending on how confident the model is.

reading.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
reading.note: introduces nucleus sampling and diagnoses repetitive degeneration

technical: Eliciting a task from a model using only a natural-language instruction, with no worked examples in the context and no gradient updates. Performance depends on whether the task, or a close relative of it, was represented during pretraining and instruction tuning, so zero-shot capability is a property of the training distribution rather than of in-context reasoning.
intuitive: You simply describe what you want and the model does it, with no demonstrations. It works when the task resembles something the model has seen a great deal of, and degrades quietly when the task is unusual.
clinical: Most bedside use of a general chatbot is zero-shot, which is also the setting where performance on rare presentations is least predictable.

reading.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
reading.note: defines the zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot evaluation settings

reading.title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
reading.note: shows a single instruction can trigger stepwise reasoning without examples

technical: A system in which a language model runs in a loop, choosing actions from a tool set, observing the results, and updating its plan until a termination condition is met. The distinguishing property is that the control flow is decided by the model rather than fixed in advance, which yields flexibility at the cost of bounded reliability, since per-step error rates compound multiplicatively across a trajectory.
intuitive: A model that is allowed to take actions and keep going until it thinks it is finished, instead of answering once. Because it decides its own next move, a small mistake early can be built upon rather than corrected, and long runs fail more often than any single step suggests.
clinical: Agentic systems that act on a chart rather than merely draft text need step-level audit logs and an explicit human checkpoint before anything is committed.

reading.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
reading.note: the reason, act and observe loop underlying most agent frameworks

reading.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
reading.note: agents with memory, reflection and planning over long horizons

reading.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
